title: Michaelmas (29 September)
hook: the feast of Michael and all angels

segments.voice: Yesterday, Exaltation: a cross honored as a tree. Your line was the tree of life.

Some universities still call their autumn term the Michaelmas term. Tradition says older calendars treated the day as a turning point of the year, when accounts were settled. And there's a folk saying, told with a straight face in parts of Britain, that you shouldn't pick blackberries after Michaelmas, because by then they've been spoiled. A feast that ended up in term names and berry picking. Its full name in some prayer books is longer and stranger: the feast of Saint Michael and all angels. Today, Michaelmas.
screen: `A TERM, A SETTLING DAY, A BLACKBERRY RULE.`

segments.voice: Michael is one of the angels the Bible calls by name. In Daniel he is "the great prince" who stands up for his people. The letter of Jude calls him "Michael the archangel." And in a vision in Revelation, "there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon." So Michael is the angel of holding the line. But the feast is for all angels, and plenty of the Bible's angels arrive without swords. In story after story they come as messengers, with news, with food, with a hand on the shoulder. Hebrews says: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." Unawares: without knowing. Some readers hear an old story from Genesis in that verse. Abraham sits at his tent door in the heat of the day, looks up, and sees three men standing near. The text doesn't say he knows who they are. It says "he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself toward the ground." He brings water for their feet, bread, a calf, milk. As the story goes on, the text has the LORD speaking to Abraham. So the feast holds two pictures: Michael standing against the dark, and strangers at a tent door who might be more than they seem. Christians differ in how much they say about angels. Catholic and Orthodox teaching speaks readily of guardian angels; some Protestants say less, and keep close to texts like the psalm: "he shall give his angels charge over thee." On this day, some simply give thanks for help they never saw coming.

Look back over the last week and find one moment when help arrived that you didn't arrange: a held door, a text at the right time, a stranger who pointed the way. Stay with it, and see their face if you can. If you pray, thank God for that help and for the person who brought it; if you don't, hold them in mind with thanks.
Michaelmas. The feast of Saint Michael and all angels, for the archangel who stands up, and for the messengers who arrive as strangers.
Your line: angels unawares. Some strangers are more than they seem. Day one thousand fifty-one, done.

howItsDone: Churches that keep Michaelmas read the scriptures of Michael and of angels, and some pray traditional prayers to Saint Michael or about guardian angels; in some places the day also keeps old customs of the autumn.
